content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes an early stopping mechanism that builds upon progressive early stopping (PES; Bai et al, 2021) to include progressive early stopping separately on the phase and amplitude spectra of 2D discrete Fourier transformed representations of intermediate layers of a deep neural network. It is evaluated on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 along with versions of these with various forms of label noise. In the fully supervised setting, the proposed approach performs about as well as PES. In the semi-supervised setting, the proposed approach generally outperforms PES by a small margin. On CIFAR-N, the proposed approach generally outperforms PES by a small margin.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
* Interesting idea. Figure 1, showing the results of training a ResNet-18 model on either the magnitude or phase spectrum of images from CIFAR-10 are quite interesting. It shows that the model trained on the magnitude spectrum is much less accurate than the model trained on the phase spectrum and that the two models begin overfitting at different epochs in the training process.

Weaknesses:
* Motivation not entirely clear. While the results in figure 1 show that the magnitude and phase spectra of the input can result in quite different model performance and early stopping characteristics, it is not obvious that the same argument would apply to intermediate representations within the model or that freezing one and not the other component of one of these representations would help model performance. In the best case, this might apply in the ResNet models evaluated, but it is also not clear whether we should expect these results to generalize to other kinds of architectures. It is also not clear why phase or magnitude would have any relationship with noisy labels.
* Low clarity makes it difficult to evaluate the contributions of the model and results. 
* Generally the improvements shown by the model are small, so it is not clear how significant they are. Statistical testing would help the reader understand these differences.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The novelty of the paper itself is rather low. In particular, it follows the structure and content of the Bai et al (2021) paper quite closely. It includes several similar figures, similar experiments, similar algorithm figure, some of the same results, etc. These similarities are largely acknowledged and properly cited, but the similarity is still high enough to reduce the novelty of the paper.

Clarity:
* The paper is not self-contained. Many details are not provided in the main body of the paper. This includes the meaning of the various noise types (Symmetric, Pairflow, Instance) and their parameters, the meaning of the different label categories in the CIFAR-N dataset(s) and any description or discussion of the properties of the various baseline algorithms. This information is available in cited papers, like Bai et al (2021).
* What is the y-axis for Figure 3?
* The use of the fully supervised case in the ablation is a bit confusing as PES performs about as well as the proposed approach, making it hard to disentangle the causes of model performance.
* The highlighting of the highest value in each column of the results table is misleading in cases where two algorithms perform similarly, which is frequent. When two values are statistically indistinguishable according to an appropriate significance test, either neither or both should be highlighted. Just using a rule of thumb estimate of 2 standard errors, this is approximately the same as the standard deviation for 5 instances, and many of the results are likely not significant.
content.summary_of_the_review: This approach to early stopping often provides small improvements in performance, although the paper itself closely follows a previous paper and is not self-contained.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper is tackling the problem of learning with noisy labels. The paper is aiming to solve the problem relying on early stopping with a suggested modification of decomposing the image into Amplitude and Phase spectrum and performing different early stopping for each. The paper demonstrates the effectiveness of the suggestion based on empirical evaluation with synthetic and real noise.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The paper empirically shows that the suggested algorithm is effective, achieving 0.5-1.5% improvement over PES  on synthetic noise (Table 1 and 2) and 0.1 - 0.6% improvement on real noise (Tables 3 &4). Overall the empirical evaluation looks relatively thorough (the comparison is performed among the most recent SOTA methods). 

Weakness:
1) The motivation -- the only motivation that the authors bring for the suggested approach (different early stops for Amplitude and Phase spectrum) is based on empirical observation of different behavior of losses of different components in Figure 1. My PhD was in low-level computer vision and I typically appreciate papers that utilize classical ideas for improving deep learning. However, I am not convinced in this case. I do not understand how decomposing the image helps to solve the problem in the label space. If the label noisy is completely random and unrelated to the image content, why would any manipulation in the image content space help?
I would suggest the authors provide an explanation for their hypothesis beyond Figure 1 experiments. The method becomes even less intuitive when applied on text in C.3 (I think there is no prior work that separated amplitude from phase for text).  

2) Paper is not clearly written and should be revised. 
2.1) It's impossible to read the first paragraph of the introduction because of the amount of references (that are highlighted with squares for some reason). 
2.2) The T in fΘT (eq. 1)  is not defined (at least I could not find this definition). It's not clear if T refers to the layers (how do you even enumerate those) or to the training epochs? I think from the rest of the section it's some kind of layer enumeration. However, the notation should be clearly defined. Moreover, an explanation should be provided how to derive the appropriate enumeration of layers for different architectures and how to optimize selection of where the disentanglement should take place. 
2.3) I would suggest to reorganize Algorithm 1 -- the common parts of the algorithm, lines 5-8 and 11- 14, should be abstracted as Algorithm 1.1 (which I assume is the main contribution of this work)  and ideally illustrated for a specific architecture (to make those clear). 
2.4) In overall, the paper can benefit from a revision. For example, it would be helpful to have Related work and Training details (at least those related to the suggested approach) in the main body of the paper. Also, Figure 3. has graphs without any axis labels. 
2.5) Please check English and other typos (marked in ***bold*** ).
Table 3: Comparison with different methods of test accuracy on ***Cloting-1M***. All methods use a pretrained ***ResNet-5*** architecture.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity and Quality -- The paper is not clearly written (see Weaknesses point 2 ) and therefore of a borderline quality. 

Novelty -- the idea of using Fourier decomposition in the deep learning setting is not new in particular, but it looks new for this specific problem of learning with noisy labels. I did not find the motivation for the idea very convincing and the achieved improvements while consistent are not large (it's also not clear which works presented in the comparison were re-implemented, which might have altered their performance).  

Reproducibility -- There is no code provided and the paper is not clear, so at this point I do not think the paper is easily reproducible
content.summary_of_the_review: In overall, while showing promising results in both Vision and Text domains, the paper does not provide sufficiently convincing motivation or theoretical foundation for the suggested idea. Also because the paper is not very clear and the code has not been provided yet, it is hard to know if the approach is reproducible. Thus, I incline not to accept the paper in its current state.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper main claim is to use frequency and phase information separately in early stopping criteria during training to avoid overfitting, especially in the case of label-noise. This is justified under perceptual considerations about the human visual system.
This results in an architectural block separating phase/amplitude spectra with DFT, then stopping selectively gradients from one of the two paths, then reconstructing the output with iDFT.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The "PADDLES" block is interesting contribution, well motivated on perceptual basis and its integration with early stopping is also well justified.
The results are better than the baselines across several tests, though in some case by a low margin. In that situation I typically like to see confidence level on the performance, not just point estimates. Results on CIFAR are a good start, larger scale experiments would have made a stronger paper.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The "PADDLES" block is novel ASAIK, and an interesting processing block. The paper is clear enough that results should be reproducible, there is a statement about "released codes" so I assume the code will be publicly available.
The paper is clear, extensive and well written.
content.summary_of_the_review: I believe this is a good paper, the motivation is interesting. I always like when a perceptual motivation translates in a new learning architectura block. Results are good for most tests, although in some cases by a small margin: in that situation it would be good to have error bands / significance tests to strengthen the conclusions. Larger scale experiments, while expensive, are also preferred to complement the CIFAR experiments that are standard for model development in this domain.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
